items.prompt: Four lunch trays are on the counter. Each tray holds 3 apple slices. The picture below shows the trays with their slices. Which two numbers describe this situation?
items.representationNote: A fully drawn equal-groups display: 4 clearly bounded tray outlines, each containing exactly 3 identical apple-slice tokens. Group boundaries must be visible so the number of groups and the amount in each group are separately countable without counting the total.

responseContract.input: touch-or-mouse tap on one option tile; no typing
responseContract.hintPolicy: learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) restate the situation in groups language, (2) ask how many trays are drawn, (3) ask how many slices are inside one tray, (4) highlight one tray and its 3 slices
responseContract.feedback: states which quantity is the number of groups and which is the amount in each group, referring to the visible display; never references speed or ability

sourceLineage.derivation: Freshly authored; representation-supported entry with factors in the 2-5 band as specified. Not adapted from any worksheet.

items.academicTarget: Interpret a multiplicative situation by identifying the number of equal groups and the amount in each group, with a full equal-groups representation visible.

items.prompt: This display shows 5 jars. Each jar holds 6 buttons. Assemble the equation that matches the display, then state the product.
items.representationNote: 5 bounded jar shapes, each containing exactly 6 identical button tokens, arranged so each jar's contents are countable. A skip-counting strip (6, 12, 18, 24, 30) is available as an optional visible intermediate the learner may reveal; it is named as a counting strategy, not as the goal.

responseContract.input: drag three number/symbol tiles into an equation frame (first factor = number of groups, second factor = amount in each group), then tap the product from a product bank; no typing
responseContract.hintPolicy: learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) how many jars, (2) how many buttons in one jar, (3) offer skip-count strip, (4) partially fill the equation frame with the first factor
responseContract.feedback: ties the equation slot to the display: 'the first factor names how many jars; the second names how many buttons in one jar'

items.academicTarget: Translate a complete equal-groups representation into the equation a x b = p and determine the product, with skip-counting available as a named intermediate strategy.

items.prompt: The equation is 4 x 6 = 24. Build a display that matches it: make the groups, then place the same amount inside every group. One of the ready-made displays below does not show equal groups — do not choose it.
items.representationNote: Construction workspace: the learner taps to create group containers and taps to add tokens into a selected container, with a live count shown per container. Three ready-made displays are also offered for comparison; one has containers holding 6, 6, 5, 7 tokens and is mathematically invalid as an equal-groups model. The invalid display must be labelled unequal in feedback, never accepted as 'close'.
items.correctAnswer: Either a learner-built display of 4 containers with exactly 6 tokens in each, or Ready display A: 4 containers of 6. Ready display B is rejected because its groups are not equal. Ready display C shows 6 groups of 4; its total is also 24 but it does not match 4 groups of 6, so it is not accepted here.

responseContract.input: tap-to-create containers and tap-to-add tokens, or tap one ready display; no typing
responseContract.validation: accepts only exactly 4 containers each holding exactly 6 tokens; reports container count and per-container count back to the learner
responseContract.hintPolicy: learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) which factor tells how many groups, (2) make that many empty containers first, (3) how many go in each, (4) fill one container as a model
responseContract.feedback: for display B: 'these groups are not equal, so this cannot be an equal-groups model'; for display C: 'this shows 6 groups of 4, which is a different situation'

items.prompt: A garden bed has 4 rows of seedlings with 7 seedlings in each row. On the left the seedlings are shown as 4 separate groups; on the right the same seedlings are lined up as a rectangle. Read the rectangle: how many rows, how many in each row, and what is the total?
items.representationNote: Side-by-side panels showing the identical 28 tokens. Left: 4 bounded groups of 7. Right: a 4-row by 7-column rectangular array with row bands lightly shaded so rows and columns are unambiguous. Row and column labels appear on tap. Both panels must be simultaneously visible without scrolling in 1365x768.

responseContract.input: tap one option tile; row/column labels revealed by tap; no typing
responseContract.hintPolicy: learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) a row runs across, (2) count the rows down the side, (3) count one row across, (4) highlight the top row and the left column
responseContract.feedback: names that the group display and the array hold the same 28 seedlings, and that the array's rows are the groups

items.phase: Phase 5 - Array construction and factor-role reasoning
items.prompt: Situation A: 3 shelves, 8 mugs on each shelf. Build the array for Situation A. Then look at Situation B: 8 shelves, 3 mugs on each shelf. Choose the statement that is true about the two situations.
items.representationNote: Array-builder grid: the learner drags a corner handle to set rows and columns, with a live readout 'rows: _, in each row: _' and the tokens rendering as they build. After the build is validated, both arrays (3x8 and 8x3) are displayed side by side with rows clearly distinguishable, along with both stated situations in words.
options: Both totals are 24, and the two situations describe different arrangements.
Both totals are 24, so the two situations describe the same arrangement.
Situation B has a larger total because 8 is larger than 3.
items.correctAnswer: Both totals are 24, and the two situations describe different arrangements.

responseContract.input: drag to size the array (must resolve to 3 rows of 8), then tap one statement; no typing
responseContract.validation: accepts only a 3-row by 8-column array for Situation A; reports the rows and per-row count back to the learner
responseContract.hintPolicy: learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) which number tells how many shelves, (2) shelves are rows, (3) set the rows first then stretch each row, (4) show a 3-row frame with the first row filled
responseContract.feedback: states that the totals match at 24 while the shelf arrangements differ; no property is named

items.prompt: Harder tier, available if you want it: 9 crates are loaded, with 8 bolts in each crate. There is no picture this time. Set the rows and columns of an empty grid to match the situation, then choose the product. (Choosing the standard tier instead keeps everything ahead of you open.)
items.representationNote: Offered explicitly as a choice tile: 'harder tier' or 'standard tier', with declining carrying no penalty and no effect on access to the transfer task. In the harder tier the array-builder starts empty with no pre-drawn tokens and no skip-counting strip shown by default; the strip remains reachable as a hint step. Standard tier presents a parallel item at 6 x 7 = 42 with a partially drawn array.

responseContract.input: tap tier choice; drag to size the grid to 9 rows of 8; tap one product tile; no typing
responseContract.validation: grid must resolve to 9 rows with 8 in each row before the product bank unlocks
responseContract.hintPolicy: learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) how many crates, (2) crates are rows, (3) reveal the skip-count strip by 8, (4) reveal the first two completed rows; the product is never given as a first hint
responseContract.feedback: verifies 72 against the grid the learner built, row by row; declining the harder tier is acknowledged neutrally with no evaluative language

items.prompt: No picture is provided for this one. A weaving frame is threaded in 7 bands, and each band carries 5 beads. Build a representation of your choice — equal groups or an array — then assemble the equation and state the product.
items.representationNote: Blank workspace with two builder modes the learner selects between: an equal-groups builder (create containers, add tokens) or an array builder (drag rows and columns). No pre-built structure of any kind. An equation frame with draggable number and symbol tiles and a product bank sits beside the workspace; both fit within 1365x768 with no scrolling.
options: Representation mode: equal groups | array (learner chooses); equation tiles: 1-10, x, =; product bank includes 12, 30, 35, 40, 45
items.correctAnswer: A representation showing 7 groups (or 7 rows) with exactly 5 in each, the equation 7 x 5 = 35, and the product 35.

responseContract.mode: free-construction plus equation assembly plus product selection
responseContract.input: tap and drag only; no typing at any assessed step
responseContract.validation: representation must show 7 equal groups of 5; equation must read 7 x 5 = 35 with the first factor as the number of bands; product must be 35; representation and equation are checked for mutual consistency and any mismatch is reported as a mismatch, never as approximately right
responseContract.hintPolicy: learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) restate the situation, (2) how many bands, (3) how many beads on one band, (4) partial representation of two completed bands; hint depth is recorded
responseContract.feedback: payoff names the mathematics: 'you interpreted a situation, represented it, and matched it to an equation and its product' — no generic reward, no comparison to age, grade, or other children

items.academicTarget: Independently construct a representation and the matching equation for a novel multiplicative situation and state the product unaided.

supportProgression: Phase 0 orientation precedes item-01: one worked situation is shown with both quantities named aloud as number of groups and amount in each group. Nothing is assessed; the purpose is shared language only.
item-01: maximum support. Full equal-groups representation visible, group boundaries drawn, situation stated in plain words, four-option selection. Hints available on request in four graduated steps.

item-02: support reduced to representation-only. The representation is still complete, but the learner must assemble the equation rather than select a description. Skip-counting strip is optional and learner-revealed, named as a counting strategy rather than the goal.
item-03: direction reverses. No representation is given; the learner constructs one from the equation. An unequal-groups distractor is present so that validity, not just totals, must be judged.
item-04: new representational form introduced with the familiar form still on screen beside it. The equal-groups panel carries the support while the array is being learned.
item-05: array support withdrawn to a sizing tool with a live rows/per-row readout. Factor roles are stressed by a swapped pair, which the learner reasons about rather than being told.

item-06: learner-initiated tier choice. The harder branch removes the picture, the pre-drawn tokens, and the default skip-count strip; the standard branch keeps a partial array. Declining is neutral and does not close access to item-07.

item-07: all scaffolding removed. Blank workspace, learner-chosen representation mode, learner-assembled equation, no worked model on screen. Hints remain reachable on request and their depth is recorded as the independence measure.

Hint policy across all items: never auto-triggered by a single wrong answer; always graduated as restate situation -> identify number of groups -> identify amount in each group -> partial representation; the product is never revealed at first hint.
Silent-struggle watch: consecutive incorrect attempts without a hint request, and idle time before abandonment, are logged at every item so the request-only policy can be tested rather than assumed.
charterConcern: Three concerns, all raised for the record rather than resolved unilaterally at this stage. First, dec-10 forbids typed numeric entry, which pushes every product response into selection from a bank. Selection permits elimination and, at item-06 and item-07 especially, a correct product can be reached without valid multiplicative reasoning. I have mitigated this by gating the product bank behind a validated construction at items 05, 06, and 07, so the representation must be correct before the product can be chosen at all — but this is a partial fix, and the selection-versus-construction accuracy gap needs to be instrumented as dec-10 already specifies. Second, dec-05 requires no reused stems or surface contexts, while the charter's own uncertainty note concedes that deliberate structural repetition is pedagogically useful for noticing pattern. I have complied strictly: seven distinct surfaces, seven distinct factor pairs, no repeated stem. The cost is that item-05's swapped-factor observation and item-07's transfer both land on structures the learner has met only once, which may understate what she knows. If the retention check in evidenceRequiredNext shows weak carryover, structural repetition with fresh surfaces should be the first remedy considered, not more scaffolding. Third, a single transfer item at 7 x 5 is a thin basis for the contract's independence claim, as dec-07 itself concedes; I have kept the factors modest deliberately so that a failure there reads as a structure or sequencing signal rather than a fact-recall one, but one item cannot separate durable understanding from within-session pattern-following, and the packet should not be read as if it can.
